title: Telescope: Improving Zero Shot Detection of LLM Generated Content By Measuring Token Repetition Probability
claim: A training-induced bias leaves a detectable signature; measuring it with a modified likelihood score cleanly separates human from machine text.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, caption under each, histogram on right
description: Three labeled panels, (a) to (c), read left to right, each with a short caption underneath. Panel (a), "Vestigial Heuristic", stacks two boxes joined by a "Train" arrow. Each box shows a wavy loss landscape with a red ball (LLM training) and a blue ball (human language). In the early-training box the red ball sits on a slope. In the mature-LLM box it has settled into a different valley. Panel (b), "Telescope Perplexity", is a flow diagram. A sequence s goes into a reference LLM, which splits into two orange outputs: Telescope Perplexity, M(s_i | s_{1:i}), and standard Perplexity, M(s_i | s_{1:i-1}). Panel (c) is a histogram of Telescope Perplexity. Human text (blue, n=24342) peaks near 10 and AI text (red, n=21613) peaks near 14, with dashed vertical mean lines. The two distributions overlap only slightly. The eye goes first to the colorful histogram.
caption: An overview of the "Vestigial Heuristic" hypothesis and measuring the average token repetition probability for the Telescope Perplexity.
abstract: Distinguishing Large Language Model (LLM) generated text from human writing is a critical and difficult challenge. While LLMs are trained to write like humans, we hypothesize that this training leaves an indelible mark. LLMs develop a particularly strong aversion to token repetition very early in training. This bias persists as a ''Vestigial Heuristic'' (a developmental artifact) that is activated in LLM-generated text, separating LLM from human writing. To probe this phenomenon, we introduce Telescope Perplexity, a metric that evaluates the token repetition of the model, $P(s_i | s_{1:i})$ . Our empirical investigation reveals that the Telescope Perplexity signature emerges early in pre-training, and Telescope Perplexity empirically enables highly effective zero-shot LLM detection. We show state-of-the-art or competitive performance across diverse datasets (including modern evaluation sets we introduce), reference models, and perturbation schemes with greater efficiency than other methods.
